description: Iranian Revolution, the hostage crisis, Iran-Iraq War and Operation Desert Storm 1991.
content_html:
The Iranian Revolution and Hostage Crisis, 1979

Since 1953, the USA had strongly supported the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose regime received American military and financial backing in exchange for oil supplies and a strategic anti-communist alliance. Many Iranians resented what they saw as American interference in their country’s affairs. In January 1979, mass protests and a revolution drove the Shah into exile. The revolution was led by Ayatollah Khomeini, a Shia cleric who established an Islamic Republic.

On 4 November 1979, Iranian students stormed the US Embassy in Tehran and took 52 American diplomats hostage. The Tehran hostage crisis lasted 444 days and proved deeply damaging to President Carter’s presidency. A military rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw (April 1980), failed catastrophically when helicopters crashed in the Iranian desert. The hostages were only released on 20 January 1981 — the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated as president.

Key Fact

The Iranian Revolution (January 1979) replaced the US-backed Shah with Ayatollah Khomeini’s Islamic Republic. The Tehran hostage crisis began on 4 November 1979 when 52 US diplomats were seized; it lasted 444 days and ended on 20 January 1981 — the day Reagan took office. It severely damaged Carter’s re-election prospects.

The Iran-Iraq War and US Policy, 1980–1988

In September 1980, Iraq’s president, Saddam Hussein, ordered an invasion of revolutionary Iran, hoping to exploit the chaos of the revolution and seize the oil-rich Khuzestan region. The USA, alarmed by the Islamic Republic’s hostility, provided significant support to Iraq during the war — including intelligence, agricultural credits, and dual-use technology that could be used for weapons development. The war lasted eight years and cost approximately 500,000 to 1 million lives before ending inconclusively in August 1988.

The United States’ support for Iraq during this war was later cited as a damaging inconsistency in American foreign policy. By backing Saddam Hussein’s regime, the USA helped build up the very military machine that would threaten regional stability less than two years after the war ended. The USS Stark incident of May 1987 — in which an Iraqi aircraft fired missiles at an American frigate, killing 37 sailors — was treated with restraint by the Reagan administration, illustrating how strongly the USA prioritised containing Iran over confronting Iraq. This context made it deeply embarrassing when Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in 1990, forcing the USA to mobilise against a regime it had recently been supporting.

Having been armed and supported by the USA during the Iran-Iraq War, Saddam Hussein turned aggressively westward. On 2 August 1990, Iraqi forces invaded neighbouring Kuwait, a small but oil-rich emirate. Saddam claimed Kuwait as historically part of Iraq and resented Kuwait’s alleged overproduction of oil that was depressing prices. The international community, including the Arab League, condemned the invasion. The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 678 in November 1990, authorising the use of force to expel Iraq from Kuwait if it had not withdrawn by 15 January 1991.

Operation Desert Storm, 1991

Under President George H. W. Bush, the USA assembled a coalition of 35 nations — including Arab states such as Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Syria — to liberate Kuwait. This diplomatic achievement was seen as one of Bush’s greatest successes. Operation Desert Storm began on 17 January 1991 with an intensive air campaign that degraded Iraqi military infrastructure. The ground offensive began on 24 February 1991 and lasted just 100 hours before Kuwait was liberated. Iraqi forces suffered heavy casualties; Kuwait was freed with relatively low coalition losses.

Key Fact

Operation Desert Storm (January–February 1991) combined an intensive six-week air campaign with a ground war that lasted just 100 hours. The coalition of 35 nations, assembled by President Bush, liberated Kuwait. Bush chose not to advance to Baghdad and remove Saddam Hussein, believing it would destabilise the region and break up the coalition.

Bush’s decision to end the war at Kuwait’s liberation rather than marching on Baghdad was controversial. Supporters argued it was consistent with the UN mandate (which authorised expelling Iraq from Kuwait, not regime change) and with preserving the Arab coalition. Critics argued it left Saddam Hussein in power and required the USA to maintain a large military presence in Saudi Arabia — which became a grievance cited by Osama bin Laden and contributed to later conflict. The unresolved question of Iraq would dominate US foreign policy for the following decade.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark “Explain a Consequence” questions on the Gulf War, go beyond describing what happened militarily — explain the political and long-term consequences: the decision not to remove Saddam Hussein left him in power; US military presence in Saudi Arabia became a source of regional resentment. For 16-mark essays on US foreign policy 1970–2000, weigh the Gulf War’s success (coalition, quick victory, liberation of Kuwait) against its unresolved legacy (Saddam remained; sanctions imposed but Iraq stayed destabilised).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew the US-backed Shah and installed Ayatollah Khomeini’s Islamic Republic. The Tehran hostage crisis (November 1979 to January 1981) lasted 444 days and crippled Carter’s presidency. The USA then supported Saddam Hussein’s Iraq during the 1980–88 Iran-Iraq War, a policy that later proved deeply problematic.
  • Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. President Bush assembled a 35-nation coalition under a UN mandate to liberate Kuwait. Operation Desert Storm began 17 January 1991 with air strikes, followed by a 100-hour ground war from 24 February 1991.
  • Bush chose not to advance to Baghdad, leaving Saddam Hussein in power. This decision, consistent with the UN mandate and coalition politics, left an unresolved Iraqi problem that would dominate US foreign policy into the twenty-first century.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Tehran hostage crisis (1979-1981).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names feature (52 US diplomats held hostage for 444 days; Iranian students stormed the embassy; failed rescue attempt in April 1980; released on the day Reagan took office) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Operation Desert Storm (1991).
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Mastering: e.g. (1) It was a US-led coalition operation of 35 nations, including Arab states such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, assembled under a UN mandate after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait; (2) It began with a six-week air campaign on 17 January 1991 followed by a ground offensive starting 24 February 1991 that lasted just 100 hours and liberated Kuwait. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the 1979 Iranian Revolution and the hostility towards the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (American support for the Shah's authoritarian regime; US intervention in 1953 to reinstate the Shah; resentment of American cultural and economic influence; Khomeini's Islamist ideology opposing Western influence) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Bush's decision not to advance to Baghdad after the liberation of Kuwait.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (Saddam Hussein remained in power; ongoing US military presence in Saudi Arabia required; sanctions regime imposed but Saddam survived; unresolved Iraqi threat shaped 1990s US policy; contributed to later 2003 invasion) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Gulf War (1991) for the USA's role in the Middle East.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Significance at the time (demonstrated US military power; successfully assembled international coalition; liberated Kuwait; restored Saudi security; US seen as a credible Middle East power) AND over time (US military presence in Saudi Arabia became a grievance; Saddam remained a problem; shaped debates about interventionism; precedent for 2003 Iraq War). Secure: One time frame well-covered. Developing: Describes the Gulf War without analysing significance. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'The USA's foreign policy in the Middle East between 1979 and 1991 was largely unsuccessful.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs evidence for failure (Tehran hostage crisis; failed rescue operation; supporting Saddam who later became an enemy; failure to prevent Kuwait's invasion) AGAINST evidence of success (Gulf War coalition; quick liberation of Kuwait; 100-hour ground war; UN mandate respected; Arab states involved). Substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes events without weighing success or failure. Emerging: Narrative.

When did the Tehran hostage crisis begin?
How long did the Tehran hostage crisis last?
When did the Iran-Iraq War begin and end?
flashcard_questions.a: It began in September 1980 and ended in August 1988.

Why did Bush choose not to advance to Baghdad after liberating Kuwait?
flashcard_questions.a: The UN mandate only authorised expelling Iraq from Kuwait; advancing would have broken the coalition.
President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003, who invaded Iran (1980) and Kuwait (1990).

glossary_terms.definition: Shia Islamic cleric who led the 1979 Iranian Revolution and became Supreme Leader of the new Islamic Republic of Iran.
The 444-day crisis from November 1979 in which 52 American diplomats were held hostage in Tehran by Iranian revolutionaries.
President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003, whose invasion of Iran in 1980 triggered the Iran-Iraq War and whose invasion of Kuwait in 1990 triggered the Gulf War.
The US-led military operation in January-February 1991 that drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait using air bombardment followed by a ground offensive lasting 100 hours.
